notes.title: Start here: a cautious Chrome autofill extension and its map
notes.body:
This repo is a Chrome Manifest V3 extension that fills job-application forms from saved profiles when you click a button. It also has a small audio recorder. Everything stays in the browser.

Read in this order:

- **docs/ARCHITECTURE.md**, the "maintained implementation map" for v0.3. Start with the "Runtime and entry points" table: it says which file owns which job (popup, options page, service worker, profile store, content script, matcher, filler, recorder).
- **ONBOARDING.md**: "Safety rules", then "Walkthrough: one Autofill empty fields click", which traces a single fill through the code with line numbers.
- Then the code the quizzes use: `src/shared/fieldMatchers.ts` (deciding what a field is), `src/content/filler.ts` (writing values and Undo), `src/background/profileStore.ts` and `serviceWorker.ts` (saving profiles), `src/recorder/engine.ts` (recording).

The ARCHITECTURE.md header warns that the older training suites under `docs/` describe earlier versions. When they disagree with the code, trust the code.

excerpts.quote: This is the maintained implementation map.
This guide is for a junior developer learning the codebase and a mid-level developer who reviews changes. Read it in order: setup, then one traced click, then the story status, then the exercises.

readMore.why: The v0.3 implementation map, section by section.
A traced fill with line numbers, plus exercises.

notes.title: Concept: how a form field becomes a mapping
notes.body:
Autofill happens in two steps run by different files.

**Matching** (`fieldMatchers.ts`). For each detected field, `mapField` looks at the field's own label, its section context and its control type, and returns a **mapping**: a `kind` (for example an email or a work-authorization question), a `confidence` (high, medium or low), maybe a `value`, and a human-readable `reason`. Helper functions build these: `skip(...)` for fields the extension refuses to touch, `review(...)` for fields the user should handle, `high(...)` for confident matches. The order of the `if` checks matters: the first rule that applies decides.

**Filling** (`filler.ts`). `fillField` takes a mapping and has its own guards before it writes anything.

When a quiz describes a field, walk `mapField` from the top and stop at the first rule that fires. Then read `fillField`'s guards in order.

excerpts.quote: if (field.disabled || field.readOnly) return result(skip("Disabled, read-only, and custom autocomplete controls are left unchanged."));
export function isReviewOnly(confidence: Confidence): boolean { return confidence === "medium" || confidence === "low"; }

readMore.why: All matching rules, in the order they are checked.
The filler's guards, native setters and Undo.

notes.title: Concept: one service worker owns the saved profiles
notes.body:
Profiles live in `chrome.storage.local` under `profileStore`. Each saved **version** has a name, an id, timestamps, a `configured` flag (is it allowed to autofill?) and a **revision** number.

No page writes to storage directly. Every read and write is a message of type `EAM_STORE` sent to the background **service worker**, which calls `performStoreOperation` in `profileStore.ts`. That function runs operations one at a time through a promise queue, so two writes never interleave.

Two ideas to keep in mind while reading `profileStore.ts`:

- **Who is asking.** The worker looks at the message's `sender`: which extension it came from, and which page URL. Not every sender is allowed every operation.
- **Which revision they saw.** A revision is a counter on each version. Find where an editor sends the revision it loaded, and read what the store does with it on a save.

The "restore" branch handles whole backups and has its own rules about ids and the `configured` flag.

excerpts.quote: Saved profiles use `chrome.storage.local.profileStore`, schema version 2. Each version has a name, ID, timestamps, `configured` flag, and revision.

| `src/background/serviceWorker.ts` | Sender-checked profile messages and installation metadata | | `src/background/profileStore.ts` | Serialized initialization, migration, reads, mutations, revision checks, and recovery |

readMore.why: Every store operation, including update, delete and restore.
The message listener and its sender checks.

notes.title: Why a "US citizen authorized to work" question goes to review
notes.body:
The label contains "authorized to work", so the `auth` test fires and this is a work-authorization question. But a saved answer is used only for a *clear* question. `clearAuthorization` is an anchored pattern (`^...$`): the whole label must read like "are you legally authorized to work in the United States". "Are you a US citizen authorized to work..." has extra words, so it fails. Line 48 then returns `review(...)` if the label is not clear, *or* if it contains any of not, without, unable, unless, except, only, citizen, citizenship. This label fails both ways. Result: a review item, "Only clear, affirmative US authorization questions can use these saved answers."

Why the others are wrong:
- Mentioning work authorization and the US is not enough; the strict pattern must match the whole label.
- The result is review, not skip; citizenship is not treated as a credential.
- Yes/No options are only checked later (line 50), which this label never reaches.

excerpts.quote: const clearAuthorization = new RegExp(`^(?:are you (?:currently )?)?(?:legally )?(?:authorized|eligible) to work in (?:the )?${country}$`).test(own);

if (!us || unknownCountry || (auth && sponsor) || /\b(not|without|unable|unless|except|only|citizen|citizenship)\b/.test(own)) return result(review(kind, "Only clear, affirmative US authorization questions can use these saved answers."));

notes.title: Why Tab B's save fails after Tab A saved
notes.body:
Each saved version has a `revision` counter. After every successful operation that is not a delete, line 84 does `target.revision += 1`. So when Tab A saves, revision 4 becomes 5. Tab B still sends `expectedRevision: 4`. The `update` case checks first: if `op.expectedRevision !== target.revision`, it throws "This profile changed in another window. Export your draft, then reload the version before saving." Nothing is written. This is **optimistic concurrency**: allow anyone to edit, but refuse a save based on stale data. ARCHITECTURE.md: conflicting saves fail with the draft preserved.

Why the others are wrong:
- Last-write-wins is exactly what the revision check prevents.
- The check throws before `configured` is touched; nothing succeeds.
- There is no merging code; a mismatch is simply refused.

excerpts.quote: if (op.expectedRevision !== undefined && op.expectedRevision !== target!.revision) throw new Error("This profile changed in another window. Export your draft, then reload the version before saving.");
if (target && op.action !== "delete") { target.revision += 1; target.updatedAt = new Date().toISOString(); }

notes.title: Why two employment "Company" fields both stay empty
notes.body:
`mapFields` first maps each field on its own, so both Company fields become `experienceCompany` with the first saved employer. Then it counts how often each education/experience kind appears. `experienceCompany` appears twice, so for both mappings it sets `value: undefined` and `confidence: "medium"`, with the reason "Repeated history fields need manual matching to the correct profile entry." The comment explains why: field ids on arbitrary sites cannot be reliably tied to profile rows, so the code will not "silently repeat entry zero, including the first row". Both fields need the user.

Why the others are wrong:
- The first field is not kept either; the rule applies to every mapping of that kind, "including the first row".
- There is no position-to-index matching; that is what the comment says cannot be done reliably.
- Repeating entry zero into both is exactly what the code refuses to do.

excerpts.quote: // Repeated history sections cannot be reliably associated with profile rows from // arbitrary IDs. Do not silently repeat entry zero, including the first row. const counts = new Map<FieldKind, number>(); for (const mapping of mappings) if (/^(education|experience)/.test(mapping.kind)) counts.set(mapping.kind, (counts.get(mapping.kind) ?? 0) + 1); return mappings.map((mapping) => (counts.get(mapping.kind) ?? 0) > 1 ? { ...mapping, value: undefined, confidence: "medium", reason: "Repeated history fields need manual matching to the correct profile entry." } : mapping);

notes.title: Why a dropdown matches the visible label before the value
notes.body:
For a select element, `fillField` first keeps the enabled options. Then it builds `labelMatches`: options whose visible text (`o.text`) equals "Yes" after normalising. Only if that list is empty does it fall back to comparing `o.value`. Here one option's text is "Yes", so `labelMatches` has exactly that option, and the value list is never built. One match means that option is chosen. ARCHITECTURE.md states the rule: "Select labels take priority over machine values".

Why the others are wrong:
- The code prefers labels, not values; values are only the fallback.
- It does not take the first match in page order; it builds the label list first.
- Ambiguity is judged inside the chosen list. The label list has one option, so it is not ambiguous.

excerpts.quote: const labelMatches = options.filter((o) => normalizeText(o.text) === normalizeText(value)); const matches = labelMatches.length ? labelMatches : options.filter((o) => normalizeText(o.value) === normalizeText(value)); const option = matches.length === 1 ? matches[0] : undefined;
Select labels take priority over machine values; ambiguous or disabled choices are rejected.

notes.title: How the recorder picks its format and chunk size
notes.body:
`start` tries a fixed list of formats in order: `["audio/webm;codecs=opus", "audio/webm", "audio/mp4"].find(this.deps.supported)`. `find` returns the first one the browser supports (the real dependency is `MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported`). If none is supported it throws. Later it calls `recorder.start(1000)`. The number is a *timeslice* in milliseconds: MediaRecorder emits a chunk of data about every second, and each chunk is appended to storage. That is why ARCHITECTURE.md says the engine "saves chunks about every second", and why failures keep the chunks already committed.

Why the others are wrong:
- The type is chosen from the list, not the browser default, and the timeslice is 1000, not 250.
- audio/mp4 is the last choice, and there is a timeslice, so it is not one blob at the end.
- webm comes before mp4 in the list, and the timeslice is 1000 ms, not ten seconds.

excerpts.quote: const mimeType = ["audio/webm;codecs=opus", "audio/webm", "audio/mp4"].find(this.deps.supported); if (!mimeType) throw new Error("This browser does not support audio recording. Use a current Chrome version.");
recorder.start(1000); this.update("recording");
saves chunks about every second

notes.title: Why the filler will not overwrite text typed after the scan
notes.body:
The scan recorded the field as empty, and `mapField` only skips fields whose `valueBefore` was non-empty. But that was scan time. Before writing, `fillField` reads the live element again: `if (element.value.trim()) return false;`. The comment says why: "A scan cannot authorize replacing anything typed since the scan occurred." The user's text is now there, so the function returns false and writes nothing.

Why the others are wrong:
- There is no append logic; the function either writes the full value into an empty field or does nothing.
- A high mapping is not written blindly; several guards run first, and this one checks the live value.
- The rollback batch only records fields that were actually filled; here nothing is filled.

excerpts.quote: // A scan cannot authorize replacing anything typed since the scan occurred. if (element.value.trim()) return false;
if (field.valueBefore?.trim()) return result(skip("Existing answers are preserved. Clear the field yourself to replace one."));

notes.title: Why a medium-confidence mapping is never written
notes.body:
The very first line of `fillField` is a guard: `if (mapping.confidence !== "high" || ...) return false;`. Any mapping that is not high, whether medium or low, returns false immediately, however good its value looks. `confidence.ts` names the policy: `shouldFill` is true only for "high", and `isReviewOnly` is true for "medium" and "low". Medium means "show it to the user for review", not "fill with a warning".

Why the others are wrong:
- Whether the field is required plays no part in this guard.
- Nothing is written, so nothing goes into the rollback batch.
- Medium items are reported for review, but they are not written first.

excerpts.quote: if (mapping.confidence !== "high" || !mapping.value?.trim() || field.disabled || field.readOnly) return false;

export function shouldFill(confidence: Confidence): boolean { return confidence === "high"; } export function isReviewOnly(confidence: Confidence): boolean { return confidence === "medium" || confidence === "low"; }

notes.title: Why a native date input becomes a review item
notes.body:
`dateMapping` checks the control type early. If `field.inputType === "date"` it returns `review(kind, "The profile has month/year only. A complete calendar date needs your review.")` before any formatting. The profile stores only a month and a year (March 2021). A native date input needs a day too, and picking "the 1st" would be inventing data. So the extension leaves it to the user. ARCHITECTURE.md lists "dates needing a day" among the things that need manual completion.

Why the others are wrong:
- No code adds a default day; the date branch returns review first.
- The "YYYY-MM" form is only used when `inputType === "month"`.
- "MM/YYYY" is the last fallback for other text inputs; a date input never reaches it.

excerpts.quote: if (field.inputType === "date") return review(kind, "The profile has month/year only. A complete calendar date needs your review."); let value: string; if (field.inputType === "month") value = `${date.year}-${String(date.month).padStart(2, "0")}`;

notes.title: Why a Gender radio group is left for the user
notes.body:
`mapField` runs its checks from the top and the first match wins. The group is enabled, is not a protected type, is not an upload or an essay, does not ask for someone else's details, and is empty. Next comes line 37: if the control is a checkbox or a **radio**, return `review("unknown", "Select these choices manually so the site's state and consent remain under your control.")`. That fires here, before the code ever looks at EEO answers. So the exact-option EEO rule only applies to selects and text controls, and this radio group becomes a medium review item of kind unknown.

Why the others are wrong:
- It is not low confidence, and "required" plays no part.
- It is a review item, not a skip; skips are the earlier lines (disabled, protected, uploads, and so on).
- The radio check runs before the EEO match, so no high mapping is produced.

excerpts.quote: if (field.valueBefore?.trim()) return result(skip("Existing answers are preserved. Clear the field yourself to replace one.")); if (field.elementType === "checkbox" || field.elementType === "radio") return result(review("unknown", "Select these choices manually so the site's state and consent remain under your control."));
Repeated history rows, radio/checkbox choices, structured addresses, dates needing a day, and ambiguous questions require manual completion.

notes.title: What restoring a recovery backup does to profile versions
notes.body:
The `restore` branch first normalises the supplied store. It then makes a map from each old id to a new `crypto.randomUUID()`, and rewrites every profile with the new id, `configured: false` and `revision: 0`. Then it reads the current data and writes it to `profileRecoveryBackup`. Only after that does it replace `profileStore`. The comment: "If backup storage fails, the original store remains untouched." ARCHITECTURE.md gives the reasons: new ids "invalidate old editors", and autofill is disabled "until review".

Why the others are wrong:
- `configured` is forced to false, and a backup *is* written before replacing.
- Original ids are replaced on purpose, so open editors cannot save onto restored data.
- Ids are not kept; every profile gets a fresh UUID as well as `configured: false`.

excerpts.quote: const ids = new Map(restored.profiles.map((p) => [p.id, crypto.randomUUID()])); restored.activeId = ids.get(restored.activeId)!; restored.profiles = restored.profiles.map((p) => ({ ...p, id: ids.get(p.id)!, configured: false, revision: 0, updatedAt: new Date().toISOString() })); const data = await chrome.storage.local.get(["profileStore", "candidateProfile"]); // If backup storage fails, the original store remains untouched. await chrome.storage.local.set({ profileRecoveryBackup: { savedAt: new Date().toISOString(), data } }); await chrome.storage.local.set({ profileStore: restored });
backs up existing saved data first, replaces version IDs to invalidate old editors, and disables autofill until review.

notes.title: Why the content script cannot update a profile
notes.body:
The listener makes two checks. First `sender.id !== chrome.runtime.id`: a content script belongs to the same extension, so its id matches and this passes. Second, `extensionPage` is true only if `sender.url` starts with the extension's own URL. The content script runs inside the job site's page, so its `sender.url` is the site's address and `extensionPage` is false. For anything other than `action === "get"`, the worker answers `{ ok: false, error: "Open Manage profiles to change profile data." }`. So only the extension's own pages can change data.

Why the others are wrong:
- Content scripts do carry the extension's id, so "Invalid sender." is not what they get.
- The worker does respond, with `sendResponse` and an error.
- A matching id is not enough; the page URL check blocks the update.

excerpts.quote: if (sender.id !== chrome.runtime.id) { sendResponse({ ok: false, error: "Invalid sender." }); return; } const extensionPage = sender.url?.startsWith(chrome.runtime.getURL("")); if (!extensionPage && request.operation?.action !== "get") { sendResponse({ ok: false, error: "Open Manage profiles to change profile data." }); return; }

notes.title: Why Undo keeps a field the user edited after the fill
notes.body:
Each rollback entry remembers the field's old value and the `afterValue` the fill wrote. `rollbackFilled` walks the entries backwards and, for each one, checks `entry.element.value !== entry.afterValue`. If the field no longer holds what the fill wrote, someone changed it since, so the loop `continue`s and leaves it alone. The user's hand edit to Email survives. Every other entry whose value is unchanged is still restored. ARCHITECTURE.md calls this "last-batch undo".

Why the others are wrong:
- Undo does not restore every field; edited ones are skipped.
- The batch is not refused; only the changed entry is skipped.
- Undo goes back to the value *before* the fill, never to the autofilled value; and this field is skipped anyway.

excerpts.quote: export function rollbackFilled(entries: RollbackEntry[]): number { let changed = 0; for (const entry of [...entries].reverse()) { if (!editable(entry.element) || entry.element.value !== entry.afterValue) continue; setNativeValue(entry.element, entry.value); dispatchChanged(entry.element); changed++; } entries.length = 0; return changed;
